subject: Clearstack business case (two-pager you can share with Celia)
message:
Rufus,

You mentioned Celia will want to see the numbers before she signs off, so I've written this to stand on its own. Forward as-is or edit.

THE PROBLEM
Lumenpath's cloud bill has grown 62% year over year while active learners grew 19%. Nobody owns the gap: engineering sees cost as finance's problem, and finance can't read the bill.

WHAT WE FOUND IN THE 14-DAY READ-ONLY SCAN
- $38K/month in idle or oversized compute, mostly staging environments that run 24/7
- $11K/month in unattached storage volumes and old snapshots
- Untagged spend: 41% of total, which is why cost can't be assigned to teams

PROPOSED PLAN
Annual subscription at $64,800, based on your current monthly spend tier. If you only act on the staging schedule and storage cleanup, the projected savings are about $35K/month, so the tool pays for itself in under two months.

WHAT IT TAKES FROM YOUR TEAM
Roughly 6 engineering hours to set up tagging policies, then a 30-minute weekly review per team lead.

I'm glad to join a 20-minute call with Celia if that helps. Otherwise I'll hold the pricing in this proposal through December 19.

Priyanka
buyer_reply: This is helpful, thank you. Celia will push on the savings estimate. Can you show how you got from $49K identified to $35K projected? She'll assume we won't fix everything.
quality_notes: Written as a forwardable business case with the buyer's own scan data, a conservative savings figure, and a clear cost of effort. The buyer's pushback is a healthy, specific objection that the seller can answer.

subject: Quorum HQ: summary of our discussion and proposed next steps
message:
Dear Ines,

Thank you for arranging Thursday's session with Dr. Lindqvist. I'm summarizing our discussion below for your records.

Current state: board materials are assembled across email, a shared drive, and a PDF compiler, typically over the six business days before each quarterly meeting. Two of Corvane's investors have asked for a single, permissioned location for historical materials ahead of the Series C.

Requirements you identified:
- Granular permissions so observers see only designated sections
- Retention of the last eight quarters of board books
- E-signature for consents, so you can stop chasing signatures by email

Quorum HQ addresses all three in the standard plan. Migration of historical materials is included in onboarding.

Proposed next steps:
1. I will send a security overview and our standard DPA by Monday.
2. Your counsel reviews the DPA (typically one to two weeks).
3. We configure a workspace in time for your March board meeting.

Please let me know whether Dr. Lindqvist would like a brief follow-up before we proceed.

Kind regards,
Wendell Haraszti
quality_notes: Formal tone fits a Chief of Staff at a pre-Series C biotech. It captures the buyer's context, ties requirements to the product without overselling, and lays out a realistic timeline anchored to their board calendar.

subject: Your team's 'where did we hear that?' problem
message:
Hey Haruki,

Quick recap since half your PMs dropped off at the 30-minute mark (no worries, I know sprint planning was calling).

The moment that landed in the demo was when Sinead searched 'manager approvals' and got 14 clips from interviews she didn't know existed. That's the problem you described: research gets done, then it lives in someone's folder and gets re-done next quarter.

For the PMs who missed it, here's a 3-minute clip of just that part. Could be worth dropping in your product channel.

Next step we talked about: a two-week trial where Sinead uploads the last 20 interviews from the onboarding redesign. If the PMs actually search it during planning, that's your signal. If they don't, you'll know it's not the right time.

Want me to set up the workspace this week?

Corinne
buyer_reply: Ha, yes, sprint planning won. Set it up, Sinead is the owner. I'll post the clip.
quality_notes: Casual tone suits the relationship. It anchors on the single moment that resonated, gives the champion something easy to share with absent stakeholders, and frames a trial with an honest success signal.

subject: URGENT - pricing expires Friday!!
message:
Hi Teodora,

I wanted to let you know that the special pricing in the proposal I sent expires THIS FRIDAY. After that the price will go up by 20% and I can't guarantee we'll be able to start your SOC 2 Type II project before your audit window.

Many companies like yours have already locked in this pricing. Don't miss out!

Can we get the order form signed by Thursday? I can send a DocuSign right now.

Thanks,
Bart
buyer_reply: Bart, we're in the middle of a vendor security review and our procurement process takes what it takes. Pressure like this doesn't help your case. I'll be in touch when we're ready.
quality_notes: Fake urgency and social proof with no substance. It ignores the buyer's actual procurement process and creates friction with a security leader who is already cautious by profession.

subject: Pipewise recap + what your CRO will ask
message:
Callum,

Short recap and then something to help you sell this internally.

What you told us: your forecast misses by 18-25% most quarters, mostly because late-stage deals slip and reps don't update close dates until the last week. Your RevOps lead spends Monday mornings rebuilding the forecast in spreadsheets.

What you saw: slip-risk scoring on your own exported Q3 pipeline. It flagged 9 of the 11 deals that actually slipped.

What Dana (your CRO) will probably ask, with answers:
- 'Will reps have to do more data entry?' No. It reads activity from email and calendar; reps don't fill anything in.
- 'How long until it's accurate for us?' The model uses your last 6 quarters on day one. Expect it to be useful in week 2.
- 'What does it cost?' For 45 sellers, list is $52K/year. Proposal coming once you confirm the seat count.

Next step you proposed: a 30-min call with Dana on the 10th. I'll bring the Q3 backtest. Confirm and I'll send the invite.

Esperanza
quality_notes: Direct and useful. It equips the champion with anticipated executive objections and answers, grounded in a backtest on the buyer's own data.

subject: After our call: onboarding without Fernando's 40-step checklist
message:
Hi Nkechi,

Thank you for being so candid on Monday about how stretched things are. Hiring 30 people in a quarter with a People team of two is a lot, and it was clear the onboarding piece keeps landing on you and Fernando at 9pm the night before someone starts.

What I took away:
- New hires regularly show up without a laptop or design software licenses ready
- Fernando's checklist has 40 steps across IT, facilities, and payroll, and nobody else can run it
- You want people to feel welcome on day one, and right now the first day is mostly waiting

What we'd set up first is just the laptop and license provisioning, triggered automatically when an offer is signed. That alone takes about 15 of Fernando's 40 steps off his plate. The welcome experience can come later once you have some breathing room.

I've attached a short note explaining what Onramp would and wouldn't change, written so Fernando can read it without a sales pitch.

If it's easier, I'm happy to talk through it with both of you over a 20-minute call. No rush on timing.

Leopold
buyer_reply: Thank you for this, honestly. Fernando read the note and said 'finally.' Can we talk next Wednesday?
quality_notes: Empathetic without being saccharine. It reflects the buyer's real constraints, narrows scope to a manageable first step, and gives the champion's colleague a no-pitch explainer.

subject: Tallyhouse proposal for Marisco Hotel Group
message:
Dear Bertrand,

Please find attached our proposal for Tallyhouse.

Tallyhouse is the leading procurement and vendor spend management platform. Our platform enables organizations to achieve best-in-class spend visibility, drive compliance, and unlock savings through intelligent automation and AI-powered insights.

Key benefits include:

Pricing is detailed on page 14. We look forward to the opportunity to partner with Marisco Hotel Group.

subject: Beacon CX: the churn pattern from your data, and a draft plan
message:
Hi Matthias,

Thanks for sending the anonymized account export before the demo. A couple of things stood out that I want to make sure you have in writing.

In your 2025 churned accounts, 71% showed a drop in weekly active users of more than 30% at least 60 days before cancellation. Your CSMs were only alerted at renewal (about 30 days out), when most of those customers had already decided.

That's the core case: Beacon CX would have flagged those accounts roughly a month earlier, while there was still time for an exec sponsor call or a re-onboarding.

I'd suggest we not over-engineer the health score on day one. Start with three signals you already trust (usage trend, open support tickets, NPS response) and add more after a quarter.

Draft plan:
- This week: you share the scoring criteria with your CS managers for gut-check
- Next week: we configure the three-signal score on your sandbox
- Week 3: CSMs use it for their Monday account reviews; we measure how many at-risk flags they agree with

Does that sequencing work with your QBR schedule?

Rashida
buyer_reply: Mostly yes. Week 3 runs into our QBR prep, so let's push that a week. Also, can we include product usage by feature, not just overall WAU? Our churn is often a single feature people stop using.
quality_notes: Leads with an insight drawn from the buyer's own data, recommends a deliberately simple start, and proposes a plan the buyer can adjust. The reply shows real engagement and a useful refinement.

subject: Draftkit next steps
message:
Phoebe,

Thanks for the time today. Appreciate it.

Per our conversation, I'll send over pricing. We'd love to get you onboarded ASAP. Can you let me know who else needs to be involved in the decision and what your timeline looks like? Also, what budget do you have allocated for this?

Thanks,
Ignatius
buyer_reply: We discussed all of that in the call. The timeline is tied to the subcontractor agreement refresh in Q2, and Maeve from legal ops is the other decision maker. Please check your notes.

message:
[Proposal walkthrough call, CFO + Controller. Goal: confirm the business case and surface any blockers before procurement.]

OPEN
'Thaddeus, thanks for making time. I know you blocked 30 minutes, and I'll keep us to 25. My goal is to walk through the proposal, make sure the numbers reflect your situation, and find out what could slow this down. Sound fair?'

RECAP THE PROBLEM (in their words)
'When we met with Yvette, the headline was that you've added 22 practices through acquisition this year, and each one closes on its own schedule. Consolidated close is at 16 days and the board wants it at 10 before you go to the lenders next fall. Is that still the right framing?'
[Pause. Let them correct. If the number changed, update the case live.]

THE CASE
'The proposal is built on three things Yvette's team measured, not on our benchmarks:
- 340 bank and card reconciliations per month, about 70% of which are straightforward matches we'd automate
- Roughly 5 days spent rolling up practice-level entries, which drops to about 1 with the standard roll-up workflow
- Two FTEs of contractor time during close, which you said you'd prefer to stop renewing'

'At the proposed annual fee of $118,000, the contractor savings alone cover about 80% of the cost. The faster close is the real point, though, because that's what the lenders are looking at.'

CHECK FOR BLOCKERS
'Two questions. First, who besides you needs to approve a contract of this size? Second, is there anything about the new-acquisition onboarding that worries you? That's usually where DSOs get nervous.'

[Likely objection: 'We're still integrating practices; is this the right time?']
'That's fair. The customers who wait usually say the opposite in hindsight: every practice you add before Ledgerline is one more to migrate later. We'd onboard the 22 existing practices in waves of five, and new acquisitions plug into a standard template.'

CLOSE
'If the numbers hold up, what would you need to see to sign by end of January? I'll put that in a one-page plan for you and Yvette.'
quality_notes: Well-structured call script that recaps the problem in the buyer's terms, builds the case from their own measurements, anticipates a realistic objection, and ends with a concrete next commitment.

subject: Patchbay: answers to the 4 technical questions from Wednesday
message:
Vikram,

You and Elif asked four things I couldn't fully answer live. Here they are.

1. On-prem ERP connectivity. Patchbay connects through a lightweight agent that runs inside your network and makes outbound-only connections. No inbound firewall rules. Install doc attached.

2. Throughput for the shop-floor sensor feed. Your estimate was ~2M events/day. That's within standard limits; we'd batch them in 5-minute windows to your warehouse. If you need real-time, it's a different tier, and I'd want to understand the use case first.

3. Who can edit production flows. Role-based permissions with separate dev/staging/prod environments. Promotion to prod requires an approver you designate.

4. What happens when your ERP is down for maintenance. Failed calls retry with backoff for up to 24 hours, then land in a dead-letter queue with alerts. Nothing silently disappears.

Elif mentioned wanting to build the order-sync flow herself in a trial. I've set up a sandbox with a mock ERP endpoint so she can start without touching production. Login details are in a separate email.

Henrietta

Cassius

subject: Shiftwell - the disruption-day scenario you asked about
message:
Hi Dariusz,

You asked the question that matters most for ground handling: what happens on a disruption day, when a storm delays 40 flights and your shift plan is useless by 10am?

I didn't give you a great answer live, so here's a better one.

When flight times change, Shiftwell recalculates staffing needs per gate and turnaround. Supervisors see which upcoming shifts are short, and can push an open-shift offer to qualified staff (ramp, baggage, or de-icing certified) who are off but within their rest-rule limits. Staff accept from their phones. Anything that would breach rest rules is blocked automatically.

What it doesn't do: it won't predict disruptions. It reacts to updated flight schedules from your operations system.

I've asked one of our airport customers whether they'd do a 20-minute call with you about their first winter on it. They've said yes, if that's useful.

Would that be a better next step than another demo?

Imogen

- 'Who updates the expected start date today, the rep or the project manager?'

WHERE WE FIT, HONESTLY
'Here's where we help: Pipewise looks at signals like how recently the GC has engaged, whether bid revisions are still coming in, and how long deals at this stage historically take for your team. It flags projects that look likely to slip before the rep changes the date.'

'Here's where we don't: if the GC's construction schedule shifts because a permit stalls, we won't know that unless someone logs it. So the model gets you earlier warnings, not certainty.'

PROPOSED NEXT STEP
'What I'd suggest is a backtest. Send me your closed and lost projects from the last two years, and we'll show you which slips Pipewise would have flagged and how early. If it's not meaningfully better than your current forecast, we stop there.'

'If it is, I think it's worth showing your CFO, Adaeze, since you said the bonding company asks about your backlog forecast. Would you want her on the backtest review?'

HANDLING 'WE'RE TOO BUSY FOR A BACKTEST'
'Understood. The export is about 20 minutes for your ops analyst. We do the rest. If even that's too much before year-end, we can pick it up January 6.'

CLOSE
'So: export by next Friday, review call the week after, Adaeze optional. Does that work?'
quality_notes: Thoughtful call script that is candid about product limitations for project-based sales, proposes an evidence-based backtest, and plans for the likely objection.

message:
[Async video, 3 minutes. Screen recording of a Patchbay workflow, voice-over. Sent to the Head of IT and two developers after a demo they joined late.]

Hi Caspar, hi Ngozi, hi Teodor. Leopoldine here from Patchbay. Since you joined Thursday's demo at the halfway mark, I recorded the part you missed, using the workflow you actually care about: stock updates from your warehouse system to the online store and the 42 physical stores.

[Click error branch]

[Click environment toggle]
This is all in a sandbox right now. Promoting to production needs an approver, which would be you, Caspar.

What I'd suggest: Ngozi and Teodor take this sandbox for a week and try to break it. I've sent credentials separately. Then let's do 30 minutes to go through what they found.

Thanks, all three of you.

subject: LAST CHANCE: Q4 pricing expires Friday!!!

subject: Patchbay — responses to your security questionnaire (v2)
message:
Dev,

Attached is our completed response to the 214-question vendor security questionnaire your team sent on the 3rd. A few items I want to flag directly rather than leave buried in the spreadsheet:

1. Data residency (Q41–44): All Patchbay workloads for your tenant would run in our US-East and US-Central regions. We do not replicate customer payloads outside the US.
2. PHI handling (Q88): Patchbay passes payloads through in transit and only persists them when you enable replay logging. With replay logging off, no PHI is stored at rest. We will sign your BAA as drafted, with one redline on the breach-notification window (we can commit to 72 hours, not 24).
3. Pen test (Q130): Our most recent third-party test closed in August. The summary letter is attached; the full report is available under NDA.
4. Subprocessors (Q162): There are six. The list and their roles are on page 3 of the attachment.

If your security team wants a live session to go through the "partially compliant" answers (there are nine), our security engineer can join a call next Tuesday or Wednesday.

Regards,
Hannah Whitlock
quality_notes: Proactively surfaces the items most likely to block a healthcare deal (PHI, BAA, residency) and is honest about the one redline and the partial answers. Organized for a security reviewer, not a marketer.

subject: Clearstack pricing — savings-based model
message:
Lucia,

You asked whether we'd consider pricing tied to realized savings instead of a flat platform fee. Short answer: yes, with guardrails.

Here's what we can do:
- Platform floor of $1,500/month so we're covered on cost to serve.
- Plus 15% of verified monthly savings above your October baseline, capped at $6,000/month.
- Savings verified jointly at month-end using your billing exports, not our dashboard.

At the savings range we modeled in the pilot ($18k–$26k/month), that lands between $4,200 and $5,400/month, versus $5,000 flat. So it's roughly neutral for us and lower-risk for you.

If that works directionally, I'll have our order form updated by Thursday.

Owen
buyer_reply: Directionally yes. Two asks: baseline should be the trailing 90-day average, not October alone (October had the Black Friday load test spike), and the cap should drop to $5,000. If you can do both, I'll take it to my CFO this week.
quality_notes: Responds directly to the buyer's requested pricing model with clear math and a verification method she controls. Short, specific, and moves the negotiation forward.

message:
[Call script — negotiation call with Gideon Park, Chief of Staff, Halcyon Therapeutics]

Opening:
"Gideon, thanks for making time. I know the board meeting is three weeks out, so I want to use this call to get to a final number and a start date you're comfortable with. Before I go through pricing, can I confirm what changed since our last conversation? You mentioned your CFO had concerns about seat count."

Listen for: whether the concern is about price per seat or about paying for board members who log in twice a year.

If it's the board-member seats:
"That's a fair concern, and honestly it's the most common one we hear from companies your size. Our standard plan counts board observers as full seats. What we can do for Halcyon is move the four observers to read-only access at no charge. That takes you from 14 paid seats to 10, which is $14,400 a year instead of $20,160."

If it's overall budget:
"Help me understand the ceiling. Is there a number your CFO has in mind, or is it more that this wasn't planned for this fiscal year?"

If they push for more discount on top of observer seats:
"I can't move the per-seat price without a longer term. What I can do is a two-year agreement at the same $14,400, with the second year locked. That protects you from the increase we're putting in for 2027."

Timing:
"Your next board meeting is December 11. For us to migrate your last two quarterly decks and have the investor portal live by then, we'd want a signature by the 24th. That's not a discount deadline; it's an onboarding one. If it slips past that, we'd still do it, but I'd suggest using your existing process for December and launching in Q1."

Close:
"What would you need from me to take this to your CFO this week?"

Notes for the rep: Do not offer the two-year option first. Lead with the seat restructure since it solves the stated problem.
quality_notes: Branches on the actual objection, separates real onboarding timing from fake discount deadlines, and gives the rep guidance on sequencing concessions.

subject: quick q on the discount
message:
Hey Ines,

Got your note. I asked about the 25% and the answer was no on that, sorry. I can probably do 10% though if that helps? Let me know and I'll send over the updated paperwork.

subject: Vaultline: auditor bundle and the March deadline
message:
Ricardo,

Following up on yesterday's call with your controller. I heard three things clearly: you need SOC 2 Type II in hand by the end of March for the Larkspur Bank partnership, you'd rather not run two vendor processes (platform and auditor), and the $62k all-in quote is $9k above what you'd budgeted.

Here's a revised proposal:

- Audit partner bundle through one of our two partner firms: $19,500, down from $28,000 because you'd be in their Q1 batch, which they price lower.
- Total: $53,500.

The trade-off is scheduling. Bundled audits run in a fixed window; your observation period would start December 15 and the auditor fieldwork would happen in the second half of February. If your team can hit the control-readiness milestones by mid-December (we think 80% of them are already green based on your integration scan), March holds.

If the December start is too aggressive, I'd rather tell you now that the price goes back up than promise a date we'll miss.

Nadia
buyer_reply: This is helpful and the number works. My concern is the December 15 start; half my team is out the last two weeks of December. Can we see the readiness list so I can judge it myself?

subject: Pipewise: where we landed
message:

subject: Onramp — proposed redlines on the MSA
message:
Dear Samuel,

Thank you for returning the MSA with your team's comments. Our legal team has reviewed them and we are able to accept most of the changes. Please see our response below.

Accepted: Section 4.2 (data deletion within 30 days of termination), Section 7.1 (mutual confidentiality), Section 11 (governing law, Delaware).

Partially accepted: Section 9.3 limitation of liability. We can increase the cap from 12 months of fees to 18 months, but cannot agree to an uncapped liability for data breaches. We can offer a super-cap of 3x annual fees for data protection claims.

Not accepted: Section 6.4 (unilateral right to audit with 5 days' notice). We propose 30 days' notice, once per year, with our SOC 2 report satisfying the audit requirement in most cases.

Please let me know if your legal team would like to schedule a call.

Kind regards,
Leah Fitzgerald
buyer_reply: Thanks Leah. The super-cap is a reasonable middle ground. On audit rights, our policy requires the ability to audit after a security incident; can we add that exception to the 30-day/once-per-year language?
quality_notes: Clear and well organized redline summary, but reads like a forward from legal with no explanation of why positions were taken and no attempt to anticipate the obvious incident-based audit exception.

subject: Yes, we'll fill out your vendor onboarding form (all 11 tabs)
message:

subject: Beacon CX — taking the pressure off the timeline
message:
Felix,

I heard you on Monday when you said the reorg has your team stretched and you're not sure you can absorb a rollout in Q1. I don't want to push a contract that turns into shelfware because the timing was wrong.

A couple of ways we could handle this:

2. Smaller first phase. License only the 12 CSMs on your enterprise segment at $2,400/seat instead of all 30. Expand at the same price within 12 months.

Which of these is closest to what you'd want?

Danielle
buyer_reply: Option 1 is attractive. I'd need finance to agree to a deferred start; they've pushed back on that before. Let me ask and I'll get back to you by next Wednesday.

subject: Draftkit order form — clause library and pricing

message:
[Negotiation call — Rosalind Tate, Controller, Ironbark Builders]

Goal: get agreement on payment terms. Price is already agreed at $36,000/year.

Open:
"Rosalind, thanks for jumping on. My understanding from your email is that the number's fine, and the sticking point is that Ironbark pays vendors quarterly in arrears and our standard is annual upfront. Is that still where we are?"

If yes:
"Okay. Here's what I can do. Quarterly billing is fine, $9,000 a quarter. What I can't do is in arrears, because the first quarter is when we do most of the implementation work. So: quarterly in advance, Net 30. Your first payment would be due 30 days after the January 1 start, so you'd effectively be paying in February for Q1."

If she pushes on in-arrears:
"I hear you, and I know that's your standard. Can I ask whether your AP policy is a hard rule or a default? Some construction firms I work with have an exception path for software subscriptions, since they're not project costs."

If it's a hard rule:
"Then let me take that back. I think I can get monthly in arrears approved at a slightly higher rate, about $3,150 a month instead of $3,000, because it changes our cash position. I'd rather tell you that now than surprise you."

Close:
"Which of those would you take to your CFO?"

Don't: reopen price. Don't offer a discount to make in-arrears go away; that's not the problem she has.
quality_notes: Narrowly focused on the actual sticking point (payment timing), explains the reason behind the seller's position, and offers a fallback with its cost stated up front.

subject: Shiftwell: per-location vs. per-employee pricing
message:
Douglas,

You raised a good point on our call: per-employee pricing punishes Meridian for your high caregiver turnover, since you're onboarding and offboarding people constantly and paying for seats in between.

I ran the numbers on a per-location model using your 22 branches:
- Per-employee (current quote): 640 active caregivers x $6 = $3,840/month, but billed on peak headcount, which was 710 last year, so closer to $4,260.
- Per-location: $175/branch/month = $3,850/month, regardless of headcount.

Per-location is about 10% cheaper at your peak and removes the turnover penalty entirely. The catch: it requires a two-year term, because it shifts the headcount risk to us.

Would two years be workable if it came with a price lock?

Aisha
buyer_reply: Two years is fine. Can we add a clause to adjust if we close or open branches mid-term? We're looking at opening three in Q3 and closing one.
quality_notes: Reframes pricing around the buyer's real operational pattern (turnover), shows the math both ways, and is upfront about the trade for the better model.

subject: pricing
message:

subject: Need your signature today to keep the discount

subject: Quorum HQ — answering your procurement team's questions

subject: Fieldnote — sizing the license to who actually uses it
message:
Jonah,

When we spoke Thursday you said the $44k quote felt like you'd be paying for 60 people to have a login when maybe 12 of them would actively tag and synthesize interviews. That's a fair read, and I think our original quote got the shape wrong.

Fieldnote has two seat types we didn't lead with:
- Contributor seats ($1,900/yr): run studies, tag, build insight reports. You'd need roughly 12.
- Viewer seats (free, unlimited): search the repository, watch highlight reels, comment.

That puts you at $22,800/year instead of $44,000. Designers and PMs who just want to pull a clip into a spec would be viewers.

The one limitation: viewers can't create their own highlight reels. If your PMs build reels today, we should count a few of them as contributors. Can you check with your research lead how many people actually make reels now?

Mira
buyer_reply: That's a much more sensible structure. Our research lead says six PMs make reels regularly, so call it 18 contributors. Send me a quote on that and I'll get it through finance.
quality_notes: Revisits the quote based on how the buyer's team actually works rather than discounting, and flags the one limitation honestly so the buyer can size correctly.

subject: Fieldnote proposal for Silverbirch Clinics

subject: Pipewise — your counter + a thought
message:

message:
[Negotiation call — Odette Marchand, CRO, Silverline Networks. Attendees: Odette, her RevOps director Kofi Asante, procurement manager Lena Wirth.]

Purpose: resolve the three open items from procurement's last email: (1) price per seat, (2) uptime SLA credits, (3) termination for convenience.

Opening:
"Thank you all for the time. I'd like to take the three open items in order of what matters most to you. Odette, is that price, or is it the termination clause?"

Item 1, price per seat:
"Our current proposal is $780 per seat for 450 seats. Lena, you came back at $600. I want to be transparent about where the room is. Above 400 seats we can go to $700. To go lower than that, we'd need a three-year term, and at three years we can do $650, fixed."

Pause. Let procurement respond. Do not fill the silence.

Item 2, SLA credits:
"Your draft asks for 10% service credits for any month below 99.9% uptime. Our standard is 5% below 99.9% and 10% below 99.5%. We've hit 99.95% for the past 18 months; the report is in your data room folder. We can accept your 10% at 99.9% if credits are capped at 25% of the monthly fee."

Item 3, termination for convenience:
"This is the hardest one for us on a multi-year price. If you want the $650 rate, we'd need the term to be firm. If termination for convenience is essential, we can include it with 90 days' notice, but the rate would be $700, since we'd be taking on the risk."

Close:
"So there are really two packages: three years firm at $650, or three years with an exit at $700. Which one would you want to take to your CFO?"

If Kofi raises the CRM migration timeline: acknowledge it, offer our solutions engineer for a separate working session, and keep it off the commercial call.
quality_notes: Structured around the buyer's open items, explains the risk logic behind each position, and collapses three variables into two clear packages for decision.

subject: Onramp and your hiring freeze
message:
Hi Theo,

I saw the announcement about the hiring pause through Q1, and I'm sorry; I know that's a hard message for a People team to deliver. I also assume it changes the math on Onramp, since the business case leaned on the 400 seasonal hires you planned for spring.

I don't want to pretend it doesn't. A few ways we could adapt:

- Scale the license to current backfill volume (around 15 hires/month) on our Core tier, $1,200/month, and step up when hiring resumes, at the same per-hire rate we quoted.
- Keep the original contract but delay the start to April 1.
- Pause the conversation until you have a clearer picture. I'll check back in late February, and only once.

Whatever you decide, the IT provisioning templates our team built for your laptop and badge workflows are yours to keep.

Jessamyn

subject: Onramp — need your PO number
message:
Bettina,

Following up again on the PO. We need it to get you set up. Can you send it over?

Kyle
buyer_reply: Kyle, I've told you twice that the PO is waiting on your company's response to our insurance requirements (cyber liability coverage of $5M). Your legal team hasn't replied in two weeks. Please chase that internally.

subject: Tallyhouse — fitting your fiscal year
message:
Desmond,

You mentioned Larchmont's fiscal year runs July to June and the board approved budget only for a $30k software line through June, but the full annual price is $46k.

Rather than discount to fit, here's a structure I've used with other schools:

- Renewal on July 1 at the full annual price, which you'd include in next year's budget request.
- I'll give you a one-page ROI summary for the budget committee in April based on actual spend data from your first five months, so the renewal case isn't built on our projections.

That gets you live before spring term purchasing and lines our contract up with your budget cycle permanently.

Desmond, does the board need to approve the renewal amount in advance, or does that go through your normal budget process?

Gwen
buyer_reply: This is helpful. Renewal would go through the normal budget process, which starts in March. If your ROI summary can be ready by early March rather than April, I'd be comfortable signing on this basis.
quality_notes: Solves a budget-cycle problem with proration instead of discount and offers evidence for the renewal case. The closing question surfaces the next approval step.

subject: Tallyhouse pricing

subject: Beacon CX — data processing addendum and subprocessors

subject: Beacon CX: let's make a deal 🤝

subject: Draftkit — the 20% and what we can do instead
message:
Felipe,

I took your 20% request seriously and here's an honest answer: I can't get there on price alone for a 60-user deployment. But I think there are two things in the proposal you're paying for that you may not need.

1. Premium clause analytics ($14,000). You told us your team's priority this year is getting NDAs and MSAs out of email threads. Analytics is valuable in year two once there's history. Dropping it now and adding at the same price later saves you $14k.
2. Dedicated onboarding ($9,000). Your team already uses a clause library in your current tool; our standard onboarding with library import is included in the base and likely sufficient.

Without both, the first-year total drops from $118,000 to $95,000, about 19.5% lower, without changing the subscription rate.

Would your GC prefer the lower number, or keep analytics in from day one?

Imogen
buyer_reply: Smart. Drop the dedicated onboarding, keep analytics; our GC wants reporting for the board in Q3. So $109k. I'll need it on a 2-year term with the same rate locked.
quality_notes: Answers the discount request by removing scope the buyer doesn't need yet, reaching nearly the same number while protecting unit price. Lets the buyer choose the trade.

message:
[Call script — Sasha Volkov, GC, Kestrel Broadcasting]

"Hi Sasha, Paul from Draftkit. Thanks for taking the call. I wanted to talk about the pricing we sent over last week.

I know you said it was higher than you expected. The thing is, Draftkit is really an investment and the value our customers get is huge. Most legal teams save something like 40% of their drafting time. And we have AI redlining, clause library, approvals, e-signature integration, playbooks, and reporting.

So I'm hoping we can find a way to make it work. What number did you have in mind?

[If she gives a number]
Okay, let me take that back to my manager and see what I can do. I'm pretty sure we can get close.

[If she doesn't give a number]
No worries. What if I could get you 15% off? Would that be enough to move forward?

Great, I'll send the updated proposal and we can get this wrapped up by the end of the month. Thanks Sasha!"

Notes: Try to close this month.
quality_notes: Polite and reasonably structured, but it leans on generic value claims and a feature list, then folds to 15% without learning why the price was a problem or trading anything.

subject: Ledgerline — nonprofit pricing and your audit season
message:
Hugo,

Thanks for being candid that the board treasurer balked at a $19k line item when the foundation is trying to keep admin costs under 12%.

Two things we can do:
- Our nonprofit program takes 30% off list for registered charities, so $13,300/year. I should have led with this; it's on me that it wasn't in the first quote.
- If you want, our team will prepare a short memo on how Ledgerline time savings show up in your functional expense allocation. Several foundations have used it to explain the spend to their boards.

I also know your audit fieldwork starts in February. If we sign in December we'd have reconciliations running for January close, which is usually the month that causes your team the most grief with the auditors.

Hugo
buyer_reply: Thank you. The nonprofit rate makes this workable. The memo would actually help with our treasurer. Can you send the order form at $13,300?
quality_notes: Owns the omission of nonprofit pricing, connects spend to the buyer's real board metric (admin cost ratio), and ties timing to audit season rather than quota.

subject: Shiftwell — final pricing
message:
Hi Lucinda,

Here is our final pricing for 34 locations:

Shiftwell Standard: $2,890/month
Annual commitment, billed monthly
Implementation: $3,500 one-time

I know you asked about waiving implementation. Unfortunately we can't do that, but we can split it across the first three invoices.

Let me know how you'd like to proceed.

Jordan
buyer_reply: Splitting it is fine. We're ready to sign but need your W-9 and certificate of insurance for vendor setup.
quality_notes: Straightforward and responsive; offers a small payment-timing concession. Lacks any reference back to the buyer's goals, but at this point in the deal that's acceptable.

subject: Patchbay — usage tiers vs. your volume forecast
message:
Emeka,

Your team's concern was overages: if the new carrier integrations go live in Q2, task volume could jump from 2M to 6M a month and the Growth tier overage rate would make it expensive fast.

Options:
1. Growth at 3M tasks/month ($3,400/mo), overage at $0.90 per 1,000 tasks. If you hit 6M, that's an extra $2,700/month.
2. Scale at 8M tasks/month ($5,200/mo). Expensive until Q2, then cheaper than Growth plus overage.
3. Growth now with a mid-term upgrade right: move to Scale anytime in the first 12 months at the same Scale price, and we credit unused Growth fees for that month.

Option 3 is what I'd pick in your seat, since you only pay for Scale once you need it. Want me to write it into the order form?

Rhiannon
quality_notes: Models the buyer's own volume forecast across options, recommends one with a clear rationale, and offers a contractual upgrade right that removes the overage risk.

subject: Clearstack — month-end pricing
message:
Hi Freya,

We're coming up on the end of our fiscal quarter and I'd like to offer you 20% off the first year if we can get the agreement signed by November 30. That would take it from $42,000 to $33,600.

I know you mentioned your team wanted to finish evaluating the rightsizing recommendations first, but I think the discount makes it worth moving forward now. We can always continue the evaluation after signing.

Let me know!
Dominic
buyer_reply: Dominic, we want to finish the evaluation because last time we signed before testing we ended up with a tool nobody used. If you can extend the trial two weeks, we'll decide on Dec 14 regardless of the discount.
quality_notes: The offer itself is clear and the timing reason is honest, but it brushes past the buyer's stated evaluation need, which the buyer then has to defend.

subject: Vaultline — the ISO add-on
message:
Hi Bart,

Quick follow-up on your question about bundling ISO 27001 with SOC 2. Yes, we can include it. It's normally $8,000 on top of the Growth plan; for a two-year agreement I can include it at $4,000/year.

A lot of the controls overlap, so your team won't double up on evidence collection; most companies our size find ISO adds 15–20% more work once SOC 2 is in place.

Happy to put both options side by side if that helps.

Selene
buyer_reply: Side by side would help. My board wants ISO for the European expansion but not until mid-2027.
quality_notes: Answers the question directly and gives useful context on effort overlap, but misses the chance to ask about ISO timing, which turns out to change the right structure.

subject: Quorum HQ terms
message:
Dear Ms. Sandoval,

Please find our terms attached. We look forward to your signature.

Pricing: $18,000/year
Term: 3 years
Payment: Annual in advance
Auto-renewal: Yes, 3-year renewal terms
Price increase: up to 10% annually

Regards,
Harlan Beaumont
buyer_reply: We asked for a one-year term and no auto-renewal on the last call. A 3-year auto-renewing contract with 10% escalators is not what we discussed.
quality_notes: Sends aggressive default terms that contradict what the buyer asked for, with no explanation, making the buyer do the work of catching it.

message:
[Negotiation call — Malcolm Agyeman, CISO, Thistledown Insurance Group. Joined by procurement analyst Wren Hadley.]

Context: Verbal yes on Vaultline Enterprise. Procurement is pushing for 25% off the $148k annual, citing a competing quote from a "lighter-weight compliance tool." Malcolm told us privately he prefers Vaultline because of the continuous control monitoring for their three regulators.

Open:
"Malcolm, Wren, thanks for the time. I know the question on the table is price, and I'm going to give you a real answer today. Before I do, Wren, can I check what the other quote includes? I'm not trying to knock it; I want to make sure we're comparing the same scope."

Listen for: whether the competing quote covers multi-framework mapping (state insurance regulators plus SOC 2 plus ISO), whether it includes continuous monitoring or point-in-time evidence collection only, and the number of integrations.

If scope is narrower:
"That makes sense, and if you only needed SOC 2 evidence collection, I'd tell you to take the cheaper option. Malcolm, you mentioned the state examiner findings last year were about evidence going stale between audits. That's the piece that drives our price, so I don't want to cut it to hit a number."

Offer:
"Here's what I can do. On a three-year term, $126k a year, which is 15% off. Plus, we'll include the regulator-mapping workshop with our compliance team, normally $12k, so your team isn't building the crosswalk themselves. If you stay on annual, the best I can do is $140k."

If Wren pushes for 25% regardless:
"I understand that's the target. I can't get there without removing something. The honest option would be dropping from Enterprise to Growth, which loses continuous monitoring. I don't recommend it for you, but it's $98k if budget is the deciding factor."

Close:
"Malcolm, which of these do you want Wren to take forward?"

Rep note: Do not disparage the competitor by name or imply their product is insecure. Let the scope comparison do the work.
quality_notes: Turns a competing-quote discount demand into a scope comparison, anchors on the CISO's real pain (stale evidence), offers a multi-year trade and an honest downgrade path, and sets guardrails on how to talk about the competitor.

subject: Ledgerline — the Net 90 request
message:
Sofia,

Your procurement team's standard is Net 90. I asked, and the honest answer is we can't go past Net 45 without our finance team adding a financing charge, which would show up as roughly 2% on the annual price.

So the choice is:
- Net 45 at $54,000
- Net 90 at $55,080

I'd suggest Net 45, but I'll paper whichever you prefer.

Desmond
buyer_reply: Net 45 is fine. I'd rather not explain a financing fee to my CFO.
quality_notes: Short and transparent about the cost of the buyer's request, lets the buyer choose, and gets a quick decision.

subject: Fieldnote — answering your legal team on recording consent
message:
Leopold,

Your legal team flagged a fair concern: Wayfarer interviews guests in nine countries, and some of those recordings will include people who never consented to long-term storage.

Here's what Fieldnote supports, and where we'd need your process to fill the gap:

- Consent capture: our scheduler can require a consent checkbox with your own language before a session is booked. Consent status is stored on the recording.
- Retention rules: you can set automatic deletion of raw video after a set period (say, 180 days) while keeping the transcript and tagged highlights.
- Redaction: names and emails in transcripts can be auto-redacted. Faces in video can't be automatically blurred today; that's on our roadmap for Q2 but I won't promise it.

What we don't do: decide which jurisdictions require what. Your privacy counsel would still set the retention period per region.

If your legal team is comfortable with that division of responsibility, I'll add the retention configuration to the implementation plan and we can keep the original pricing.

Yasmin
quality_notes: Treats the legal concern seriously, is precise about what the product does and doesn't do (including a roadmap item she won't promise), and clarifies responsibility boundaries.

subject: URGENT: Pipewise renewal of pricing
message:
Imani,

I need to let you know that our prices are going up 18% on January 1. If we don't get your signature before then, your quote will be repriced at the new rate. I would hate for you to miss out on this pricing.

Additionally, if you sign by December 15, I can include our premium forecasting module at no additional cost for the first six months.

Please confirm by end of week so I can get the paperwork started.

Carter
buyer_reply: Is the January increase published anywhere? Our procurement team will ask for confirmation, and I'd rather not present a deadline that turns out to be soft.
quality_notes: The price increase may be real and the bundled offer is concrete, but the message gives no proof, no link to the buyer's priorities, and a pushy tone that invites skepticism.

subject: Onramp — security questionnaire follow-up items
message:
Dear Gareth,

Thank you for confirming receipt of our completed security questionnaire. Your team followed up with three clarification requests, which I've addressed below.

1. Privileged access: Onramp's production environment uses just-in-time access with mandatory approval and session recording. No standing administrator access exists. Access logs are retained for 13 months.
2. Credential handling during provisioning: Onramp never stores end-user passwords. Account creation in downstream systems uses SCIM or the target system's API with scoped service tokens, which are stored in a managed secrets vault and rotated every 90 days.
3. Employee departures: Deprovisioning revokes access in connected systems within five minutes of the HR termination event. We can provide a sample audit trail from a test tenant.

We hope this resolves the outstanding items. If your security team would like to review the sample audit trail together, our security engineer is available Tuesday at 10:00 or Thursday at 14:00.

Kind regards,
Marisol Quintero
buyer_reply: Thank you. Item 2 resolves our main concern. Please send the sample audit trail; we'll review async and should be able to close the questionnaire by Friday.
quality_notes: Precise, technically credible answers aimed at a financial-services security reviewer, with a concrete offer of evidence and specific times.

subject: Tallyhouse — tying price to the savings we projected
message:
Tamsin,

You were skeptical of our projected 4% reduction in indirect spend, which is fair; every vendor in this category promises savings. So let's put some of our fee at risk.

Proposal:
- Base fee: $72,000/year (down from $96,000).
- Performance fee: if verified indirect spend savings exceed $600,000 in the first 12 months, an additional $24,000 is due. If not, it isn't.
- Measurement: your FP&A team's numbers, comparing the 12 months before go-live to the 12 months after, adjusted for headcount.

If we're right, you pay what you would have paid. If we're wrong, you pay 25% less.

Would your FP&A lead be willing to agree a methodology with us up front?

Ellis
buyer_reply: I like the structure. FP&A will want to exclude capital projects and anything under the new hotel openings. Let me set up a call between them and your team.
quality_notes: Answers skepticism by putting part of the fee at risk on the buyer's own measurement, with a clear payoff logic and a concrete next step.

subject: Beacon CX contract
message:
Hi Alistair,

Attached is the contract with the changes we talked about. Let me know if you have any questions or if anything looks off.

Thanks!
Gemma
quality_notes: Fine for a simple handoff, but doesn't summarize which changes were made, so the buyer has to diff the contract himself and errors may slip through.

subject: Draftkit — our response regarding indemnification
message:
Dear Noor,

Thank you for your detailed redline of the Draftkit Master Subscription Agreement. As a legal technology vendor, we recognize that our buyers read our paper more carefully than most, and we appreciate the precision of your comments.

Regarding Section 10 (Indemnification): we accept your expansion of our IP indemnity to cover claims arising from AI-generated suggestions, provided that the indemnity does not extend to content materially modified by your users after generation. We have proposed language to that effect.

Regarding your request for mutual indemnification for data misuse: we accept, subject to the liability cap in Section 11.

Regarding Section 11 (Limitation of Liability): we propose a general cap of 12 months' fees and a super-cap of 2x annual fees for breaches of confidentiality and data protection obligations.

Our redline is attached. We would welcome a call between counsel to close the remaining items.

Respectfully,
Rupert Fairweather
buyer_reply: Rupert, the AI indemnity carve-out is acceptable. On the cap, we need 3x for data protection given the privileged material involved. If you can agree, we can sign this month.
quality_notes: Engages a GC on her own terms with specific, reasoned positions, accepts the novel AI indemnity with a sensible carve-out, and keeps the remaining gap narrow.

message:
[Negotiation call — Terrence Holt, COO, Granite Ridge Distribution]

"Hi Terrence, it's Bianca from Shiftwell. Do you have ten minutes?

Great. So I saw your email about the pricing. You said it's too high. I get that. Everyone says that at first! But I really think once you see how much time your managers save, you'll see it pays for itself.

Our pricing is $7 per employee per month. For your 1,800 warehouse staff, that's $12,600 a month. But think about it: if each of your 60 shift managers saves 5 hours a week on scheduling, that's 300 hours a week. At $35 an hour that's over $10,000 a week, so you're saving way more than you're spending.

So does that make sense?

[If he still says it's too high]
Okay. Let me see what I can do. Would 10% off help? I could probably get that approved.

[If he says he needs to talk to finance]
Totally understand. When can we schedule a follow-up with them?

Thanks Terrence!"

Notes: try to close this week.
quality_notes: Dismisses the price objection with 'everyone says that,' uses unverified ROI math the buyer never agreed to, and caves to a discount immediately without understanding the real concern.

subject: Patchbay — response to FedRAMP and hosting questions
message:
Marcus,

Your security team asked whether Patchbay is FedRAMP authorized. It is not. I want to be direct about that rather than wait for it to surface in the questionnaire.

What we can offer:
- A single-tenant deployment in a US-only government cloud region, operated by US persons, which several of our state and local customers use.
- A SOC 2 Type II report and a completed NIST 800-53 moderate control mapping.
- Contractual commitment to keep CUI out of logs.

If any of your Patchbay workflows will touch federal contracts that require FedRAMP Moderate, we're not the right vendor for those, and I'd rather you know now. If your initial scope is the internal HR and finance integrations you described, the single-tenant option may meet your requirements.

Would it help to have our compliance lead walk your security team through the control mapping?

Ingrid
buyer_reply: Appreciated. Initial scope is internal systems only, so this could work. Yes, please set up the walkthrough; I'd like our FSO in the room.
quality_notes: Discloses a deal-relevant gap early, scopes where the product fits and where it doesn't, and offers a path that respects the buyer's compliance obligations.

subject: Clearstack — pricing based on spend
message:
Hi Penelope,

Thanks for the call. As mentioned, Clearstack pricing is based on a percentage of your managed cloud spend. At roughly $4.2M/year in spend, our standard rate would be 2.5%, or about $105,000/year.

You asked about a lower rate. We do have volume tiers; above $5M it drops to 2%. If you expect to cross $5M during the contract, we could apply the 2% from day one on a two-year term.

Let me know what you think.

Tobias
quality_notes: Clear explanation of pricing mechanics and a reasonable conditional offer, but doesn't confirm whether the buyer actually expects to cross $5M or tie the price back to expected savings.

subject: Quorum HQ — portfolio company pricing
message:
Rowan,

You mentioned something on our call that I keep thinking about: Fernhill would want Quorum HQ for its own LP reporting, but the bigger pain is that 14 of your portfolio companies send board decks in 14 different formats.

Instead of discounting the firm license, here's a different structure:
- Fernhill firm license: $16,000/year (list).
- Portfolio program: any Fernhill portfolio company gets Quorum HQ Starter at 40% off for two years, and their board packages flow into your portal automatically.
- Fernhill pays nothing for the portfolio companies; they each contract directly.

That way your partners get standardized board materials across the portfolio, and your companies get a better rate than they could negotiate alone.

Is that something your partners would want to offer?

Annika
buyer_reply: That's genuinely interesting. Our ops partner has been trying to standardize board reporting for two years. Let me bring it to Monday's partner meeting.
quality_notes: Shifts the negotiation from discount to a structure that solves a bigger problem the buyer mentioned, creating value for both sides.

subject: Ledgerline — can you sign by the 30th?
message:
Hi Gloria,

It's the end of our quarter and I'm trying to hit my number. If you can sign by November 30, I'll throw in an extra 10%. I know it's tight but I'd really appreciate the help.

Thanks,
Brandon
buyer_reply: Brandon, I appreciate the honesty, but my procurement calendar doesn't care about your quarter. We're on track for mid-December.
quality_notes: Asks the buyer to accelerate for the seller's quota with no business reason for her; honest, but it gives away discount and gets nothing.

subject: Fieldnote — multi-year enterprise agreement
message:
Callum,

Following our conversation with your procurement director, I'm pleased to share the revised enterprise terms:

- Three-year agreement, 80 contributor seats, unlimited viewers.
- Year 1: $144,000. Year 2: $152,000. Year 3: $160,000.
- Seat expansion during the term at the year-one per-seat price.
- Data export in open formats at any time, not only at termination.

The modest annual increase replaces the 7% uplift in our standard terms. Procurement asked about Net 60, which we can accept.

I'd appreciate knowing whether this aligns with your budget planning for FY27.

Best regards,
Daphne
quality_notes: Clear terms with sensible concessions, but it reads as a standard offer letter; doesn't tie the multi-year commitment to the research program's goals or say why the increases are justified.

subject: The good news, the bad news, and the paperwork
message:
Hi Sunita,

Good news: your CFO's ask for quarterly billing is approved. $7,250 a quarter, in advance.

Bad news: the 30% discount is not. I got to 12% for an annual term, which is $25,520 for the year, and that's the end of the line.

The paperwork: our DPA is attached with the two changes your counsel asked for, both accepted.

If you want to sign before your audit kickoff on January 12, we need the order form by December 20 to get your integrations connected and give your team three weeks of evidence collection before the auditor arrives.

Kieran
buyer_reply: Ha, appreciated the format. 12% is fine. I'll get the order form signed this week.
quality_notes: Light framing makes a mixed answer easy to read, gives specifics on every open item, and connects the deadline to the buyer's own audit date.

subject: Onramp — before we talk discount
message:
Rashid,

You asked for 20% off before your leadership meeting. Before I go back to my team, could I ask what the 20% is anchored on? If it's a competing quote, I'd like to understand the scope; if it's a budget ceiling, I'd rather redesign the package to fit than cut and leave you with something underpowered.

The two biggest cost drivers in your quote are the IT provisioning connectors (we included 12) and the custom workflow build for your partner-track hires. If either is a nice-to-have for year one, we can make the number work without a blanket discount.

Can you let me know which it is by Thursday?

Fiona
buyer_reply: It's a budget ceiling: $38k. The partner-track workflow is the reason we picked you, so that stays. We could drop to 8 connectors.
quality_notes: Diagnoses the reason behind the discount request before conceding and names the levers, which gets the buyer to reveal both the ceiling and his priorities.

subject: Pipewise — final offer, please respond
message:
Emil,

This is my final offer. I've gone as low as I can go: $28,500 for 40 seats. I have sent four emails about this and haven't heard back. I need to know by tomorrow if you're moving forward or not, otherwise I'll have to close out this opportunity.

Please respond.

Jada
quality_notes: Frustrated, guilt-laden tone and an arbitrary deadline after a silent buyer; it doesn't try to diagnose the silence and reads as a threat.

subject: Shiftwell — revised order form with union provisions
message:
Ignatius,

Attached is the revised order form reflecting the two items raised by your labor relations team:

1. Seniority-based shift bidding is enabled for the 41 unionized locations at no additional cost.
2. Shiftwell will retain schedule change history for seven years to support grievance proceedings, rather than our standard three.

Pricing is unchanged at $5.40 per employee per month for 2,300 employees, on a two-year term with annual billing.

Please note that item 2 required a small change to our data retention addendum, which is also attached for your counsel's review.

Regards,
Noelle
quality_notes: Accurate and well organized for a formal buyer, but purely transactional; doesn't confirm signing timeline or check whether the union provisions fully resolve labor relations' concerns.

subject: Re: Patchbay — 'the competitor is 40% cheaper'
message:
Priyanka,

Thanks for sharing that the open-source-plus-hosting route your team priced comes in about 40% under our quote. I believe it.

Where I'd push back is on what the comparison leaves out. In your architecture review, your team listed three requirements: field-level encryption for card data in transit, replay with PCI-scoped log retention, and on-call support for the payment-reconciliation flows. In the self-hosted path, those are your engineers' responsibility. At your loaded engineering cost, it takes about half an FTE to own that before it's cheaper.

I can't match a 40% gap. I can offer $64,000/year instead of $71,000 on a two-year term, and I'll include a quarterly architecture review with our solutions team.

If your team has done the build math and still prefers self-hosting, I'd understand.

Hamish
buyer_reply: Fair challenge. Our platform lead estimated a third of an FTE, not half, but you're in the right zone. Let me bring $64k back to the team.
quality_notes: Engages a build-vs-buy comparison with the buyer's own stated requirements instead of dismissing it, makes a modest concession tied to term, and leaves room for the buyer to disagree.

subject: Clearstack quote
message:
Hey Eamon,

Here's the updated quote you asked for: $68k for the year with the Kubernetes cost allocation module included. That's about 8% lower than before.

Let me know if this works or if you want to hop on a call!

Valentina
buyer_reply: Thanks. Does the $68k cover the second AWS org we're consolidating in March, or would that be billed separately?
quality_notes: Quick and responsive with the requested change, but doesn't clarify scope (which accounts are covered), forcing the buyer to ask the obvious question.

subject: Quorum HQ — price expires tomorrow, act now
message:
Hi Desmond,

Our special startup pricing expires tomorrow at midnight! Don't miss out on $6,000/year for Quorum HQ (normally $9,600).

Quorum HQ helps CEOs like you impress your board with beautiful, professional board decks, secure document sharing, e-signatures, investor updates, cap table views, and more.

Click here to sign now and lock in your savings!

Leonie
quality_notes: Mass-marketing tone and a countdown deadline at the negotiation stage, with a feature list and a 'click here' CTA instead of addressing anything specific to the buyer's deal.

message:
[Negotiation call — Haruto Nishida, Procurement Lead, Redcliff Auto Components]

Background: Haruto is a professional negotiator who will run us through Redcliff's standard supplier playbook (multiple rounds, "best and final" requests). Price is $88k/year. He has asked for 18% off, Net 90, and a most-favored-customer clause.

Opening:
"Haruto, I appreciate how organized your process has been. I'd like to make this efficient for both of us, so I'll be direct about which items have room and which don't."

Item 1, MFC clause:
"We don't sign most-favored-customer clauses with anyone. It's not a negotiating position; it's company policy, and I'd be misleading you if I said otherwise. What I can give you is a renewal cap: no more than 5% annual increase for three years."

Item 2, payment terms:
"Net 90 we can do if billing is annual. That one's fine."

Item 3, price:
"On price, here's where we are. 8% on a one-year term, 14% on two years. To go further, I'd need something in return, like a published case study once you're live, or a reference call twice a year. That's worth a few points to us."

If he asks for 'best and final':
"I understand you need to ask. My answer won't change on a second round, so I'd rather you have my real best now: 14% on two years, plus 3% for the case study. 17%. That's where it ends."

Listen for: whether Redcliff's internal approval depends on hitting a specific percentage. If 18% is a scorecard metric, ask whether a free month of services (implementation credit) counts toward it.

Close:
"What would you need to see to get this into your approval cycle this month?"

Rep note: Stay warm. Haruto's job is to push; don't take it personally, and don't negotiate against yourself between rounds.
quality_notes: Prepares the rep for a professional procurement negotiator: separates policy from negotiable items, ties every concession to a trade, and preempts the 'best and final' round.

subject: Beacon CX — tiering the license by account segment
message:
Gabriela,

Your concern was that paying the same per-account price across 4,000 accounts doesn't make sense when 3,200 of them are small schools on self-serve plans that your team rarely touches.

Proposed tiers:
- Strategic and mid-market accounts (800): full health scoring, playbooks, and CSM workspace, $9 per account per month.
- Self-serve accounts (3,200): automated health scoring only, used to trigger digital campaigns, $1.50 per account per month.

That's $12,000/month vs. $26,000 under the flat model.

The self-serve tier won't show up in your CSMs' daily views, which I think is what you'd want. Is that right, or do you have a scaled CS team that works the long tail?
buyer_reply: We do have two scaled CSMs who work the long tail. Could they get the full workspace on a subset of those accounts?
quality_notes: Restructures pricing around the buyer's account segmentation, shows the impact clearly, and asks a question that uncovers an operational detail affecting the deal design.

subject: Draftkit — 3 years or nothing?
message:
Marguerite,

Your procurement team asked whether we'd accept a one-year term at the three-year price. We won't. The three-year price reflects the reduced risk of a longer commitment.

Price stays at $92,000/year for one year or $81,000/year for three years.

Thanks,
Stellan
quality_notes: Clear and honest about the policy, but blunt to the point of curt, and misses an easy middle option (two years, or a three-year term with an early exit) that could keep momentum.

subject: Ledgerline — consolidated proposal for procurement
message:
Dear Constantin,

As requested, below is a single summary of the agreed commercial terms for your procurement and legal teams.

Subscription: Ledgerline Enterprise, 11 legal entities, $138,000/year.
Term: 36 months. Pricing fixed for the term.
Payment: Annual in advance, Net 60.
Implementation: $22,000 fixed fee, payable in two milestones (kickoff and first close completed in Ledgerline).
SLA: 99.9% uptime with service credits per Schedule B.
Exit: Data export in standard formats within 30 days of request; 90-day transition assistance at no charge.

Open items: none on the commercial side. Your counsel has the MSA with two remaining comments on Sections 8.2 and 12.4, which our counsel will respond to by Friday.

Respectfully,
Philippa Ngata
quality_notes: A clean, consolidated term summary that procurement and legal can rely on, with milestone-based implementation fees and clear ownership of the remaining open items.

subject: Fieldnote pricing!!
message:
Hey Tilly!!

So great chatting yesterday! I talked to my boss and we can do a crazy deal for you guys!! 35% off if you sign this week. This is honestly the best discount I've ever been able to give anyone lol. Let me know and I'll send DocuSign!!

Cassius
buyer_reply: Cassius, Aldergate requires a third-party risk review for any new vendor storing customer data, which takes 6-8 weeks minimum. A signature this week isn't possible, and a discount this large makes me wonder about the original price.
quality_notes: Overly casual for a large bank, offers a huge discount without reason, and ignores the third-party risk process; the size of the discount undermines credibility on list price.

subject: Vaultline — where we can and can't flex
message:
Gunnar,

I know you've been pushed hard from both sides: your CEO wants SOC 2 by Q2 for the enterprise deal, and your CFO wants this under $20k. I'd like to make it easier to defend internally.

Where we can flex: we can start you on the Starter tier at $17,500, which covers SOC 2 for your current 14 integrations. If the enterprise deal closes and you need ISO or HIPAA later, you'd upgrade at that point.

Where we can't: the Starter tier doesn't include the auditor-ready policy pack. Your team would write or adapt policies yourselves, which probably takes 2–3 weeks of someone's time.

I'm happy to share what policies other logistics companies had to write, so you can estimate the lift before deciding.

Adaeze
quality_notes: Empathetic framing and honest trade-offs, but the offer feels underdeveloped; it doesn't quantify whether Starter actually gets him to Q2 or mention any multi-year path.

message:
[Negotiation call — Esperanza Valdivia, IT Director, Sunfield Medical Group]

"Esperanza, hi, Lorcan from Onramp. I'm calling about the order form. I saw you sent back some redlines. I don't think we can accept most of those, honestly. Our legal team is pretty strict.

Anyway, I also wanted to mention we're running a promotion: if you sign this month you get the Okta-style SSO connector pack for free. Well, not Okta, our version. It's really good.

So can you get the redlines dropped and get this signed by the 30th?

[If she objects]
I hear you. Let me see what legal can do, but I can't promise anything.

[If she asks about the BAA]
I'll have to check on that.

Okay, thanks Esperanza, talk soon."

Notes: Push hard for month-end.
quality_notes: Dismisses redlines without specifics, pushes an irrelevant promotion, and has no answer prepared on the BAA, which is fundamental for a healthcare buyer.

subject: Pipewise — a pilot clause instead of a discount
message:
Bertrand,

You told me your hesitation isn't really the $54k; it's that your last forecasting tool never got adopted and your CRO is wary of a repeat.

So rather than discount, I'd like to make the risk smaller:
- Full annual contract at $54k.
- 90-day adoption checkpoint: if fewer than 70% of your 48 reps have submitted a forecast call in Pipewise in at least 8 of the first 12 weeks, you can terminate and we refund the unused nine months.
- We assign a customer success manager from day one to run the rep enablement with your sales managers.

That puts the adoption risk on us, where I think it belongs if we're confident.

Does that help with your CRO?

Seraphina
quality_notes: Identifies the buyer's real hesitation (adoption risk, not price) and addresses it with a measurable exit clause instead of a discount.

subject: Patchbay startup program
message:
Hi Zoltan,

Good news: you qualify for our startup program since you're under 200 employees and Series B. That gives you 50% off Growth for the first year ($1,450/month instead of $2,900). Year two goes to standard pricing.

Let me know if you'd like me to send the order form.

Delphine
quality_notes: Clear, useful pricing news, but doesn't flag the year-two jump clearly enough to avoid a renewal shock, and doesn't ask anything to move the deal forward.

subject: Shiftwell: proposal
message:
Dear Naledi,

Following up on our proposal. As we discussed in our previous meeting, Shiftwell provides comprehensive scheduling, time and attendance, labor forecasting, compliance management, shift swapping, messaging, and reporting for hospitality businesses of all sizes. Our platform is used by thousands of businesses worldwide and our customer satisfaction scores are industry-leading.

Pricing for your 620 employees is $4,340/month on an annual agreement. We are confident Shiftwell will deliver significant value to Seabright.

We look forward to hearing from you.

Yours sincerely,
Bartholomew Quist
quality_notes: Re-pitches features to a buyer already in negotiation, offers no response to any open item, and closes passively with no next step.

subject: Clearstack — payment terms and the BAA
message:
Sanjay,

Two updates:

1. Our BAA is signed and attached. Clearstack only processes billing metadata and resource tags, not PHI, but we signed it because your policy requires one for any cloud-touching vendor.
2. Payment terms: your finance team asked for semiannual billing. Approved at the same annual price, $46,000, billed $23,000 in January and July.

That should clear both items your procurement team listed. Anything else on their side?

Ottilie
quality_notes: Efficient and closes out both listed items, but misses the chance to confirm the signing date or anything else the buyer needs for internal approval.

subject: Quorum HQ — the security review and your board date
message:
Cordelia,

Your IT security team sent 38 follow-up questions on our questionnaire, mostly about how board materials are encrypted and who at Quorum can access them. I've answered all 38 in the attached sheet, but two answers will matter most to your general counsel:

- Board books are encrypted with per-customer keys. Quorum support staff cannot open document contents; they can see file names and metadata only, and only with your admin's time-boxed approval.
- Director devices: if a director loses a tablet, your admin can remotely revoke access and wipe cached documents from the Quorum app.

On timing: your January 22 board meeting is the one you wanted on Quorum. Working backward, we'd need the security review closed by December 19 and the order form signed by January 5 to load the deck and train your two board liaisons.

If the review can't close by the 19th, I'd suggest we target the April meeting instead rather than rush your directors onto a new tool.

Matthias
buyer_reply: This is exactly what our GC needed. I think we can close the review by the 19th. I'll push security on it today.
quality_notes: Pulls the two answers that matter to the decision-maker out of a long questionnaire, ties timing to the buyer's board calendar, and offers a sensible fallback instead of forcing a rushed launch.

subject: Tallyhouse: discount approved
message:
Margot,

Your 15% discount is approved. New price: $51,000/year. Contract attached. Please sign by Friday.

Wendell
buyer_reply: Thanks. I'll need the contract to reflect the Net 60 terms we discussed too; the attached version still says Net 30.
quality_notes: Gets the good news across quickly, but the attached contract is missing an agreed term, and the 'sign by Friday' deadline has no stated reason.

message:
[Negotiation call — Thaddeus Mwangi, VP Customer Success, Northstar Mobile. Also on: procurement director Elise Varner.]

Context: Northstar wants a 3-year enterprise agreement for 140 CSMs, but procurement has asked for (a) a 30% discount, (b) the right to reduce seats by up to 25% annually, and (c) Net 75 terms. We can live with (c). (a) and (b) together are not workable; one or the other is.

Opening:
"Thaddeus, Elise, thanks for making time. I'd like to start with what we can agree on and then spend most of the time on the piece that's genuinely hard."

Agreed item:
"Net 75 is fine. I'll confirm that in the order form today."

The hard part:
"The 30% discount and the 25% annual seat reduction are both reasonable asks on their own. Together, they mean we'd price for 140 seats and potentially be paid for 79 by year three. So I'd like to offer two packages and let you choose."

Package A, flexibility:
"List minus 15%, with the right to reduce seats by up to 20% at each anniversary. This fits if you expect the CS reorg to shrink the team."

Package B, price:
"List minus 28%, with seat count fixed at a minimum of 125 for the full term, and the right to add seats at the same rate."

Discovery question before they choose:
"Thaddeus, what's your honest view of headcount for CS over the next three years? If you're planning to grow with the 5G business customers, B is clearly better. If the team is likely to shrink, A protects you."

If Elise asks for both:
"I understand why you'd ask. I can't put both in front of our deal desk with a straight face. What I can add to either package is a free health-model tuning engagement with our data science team in year one."

Close:
"Which package would you like me to formalize?"

Rep note: Let Thaddeus answer the headcount question; it's information procurement may not have.
quality_notes: Concedes the easy item early, explains why the two hard asks compound, frames two clean packages, and uses a discovery question that brings the business owner's knowledge into a procurement-led negotiation.

subject: Draftkit — renewal cap and the AI usage question
message:
Benedikt,

Two items from your procurement team's latest round:

1. Renewal uplift cap. They asked for 3%; our standard is 7%. I can do 4% if the initial term is two years, or 3% on a three-year term. I'd rather not do 3% on two years; that's the one combination our finance team won't approve.

2. AI usage limits. Your team wanted to know whether heavy redlining weeks (like your annual supplier contract refresh in May) could push you over the included AI review volume. On Enterprise, the included volume is 25,000 document reviews per year. Your projection was about 14,000. If you exceed it, overage is billed at $0.40 per review, but we don't charge until you're 20% over, so May won't trigger anything unless volume nearly doubles.

If the 4% on two years works, I'll send a clean order form with both points reflected.

Ophelia
buyer_reply: 4% on two years works. Please also add the 20% overage buffer explicitly in the order form; procurement won't rely on an email.
quality_notes: Gives procurement precise, conditional answers, addresses an operational concern with the buyer's own volume numbers, and makes clear which combination is off the table.

subject: Pricing increase coming
message:
Hi Anouk,

Just wanted to let you know prices are going up soon so now is a great time to lock in. We have a lot of customers signing right now and I wouldn't want you to miss out. Clearstack can save you up to 40% on your cloud bill!

Are you ready to move forward?

Jasper
quality_notes: Vague 'prices going up soon' urgency, unsupported savings claim, and herd-pressure language, with nothing about the buyer's actual negotiation items.

subject: Ledgerline — the bank feed question before you sign
message:
Hi Lachlan,

Before you route the order form, one thing to clear up from your last email: you asked whether pricing changes if you add the two new credit card programs next year. It doesn't. The $29,400/year covers unlimited bank and card feeds; what we price on is legal entities (you have three).

If you acquire the Portland store as a separate entity, that would add $4,200/year, prorated from whenever it joins.

Anything else your CFO wants spelled out in the order form?

Imara
buyer_reply: That's the clarity I needed. No other questions; routing to the CFO this afternoon.
quality_notes: Answers the buyer's specific pricing question clearly and pre-empts a related one, though it's mostly a clarification rather than an active negotiation move.

subject: Your Ledgerline renewal and the close numbers behind it
message:
Hi Desmond,

Your Ledgerline agreement renews on January 31, so I wanted to get ahead of it with something more useful than an invoice.

I pulled your team's numbers for the last four closes. Average days-to-close went from 9.5 in Q1 to 5 in Q3, and the share of reconciliations matched automatically is sitting at 87%, up from 61% at go-live. The remaining manual work is concentrated in two places: the intercompany accounts between Harrowfield and the cold-storage entity, and the vendor credit memos coming out of your AP system.

For the renewal itself, I'm proposing the same tier and seat count (8 users) with no price change. If you want to tackle intercompany next year, that's a configuration project rather than an upgrade, and our solutions team can scope it at no cost.

Could we grab 25 minutes the week of December 8 to confirm the renewal and talk through whether intercompany is worth prioritizing?

Best,
Marisol
